K-368.title: 2D Shapes Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-368.metaDescription: 2D shapes worksheet: six cards, each a flat shape beside three names. Circle, square, triangle or rectangle, some turned or skinny. Free kindergarten PDF.
K-368.p1: Six numbered cards fill this kindergarten page, two across and three down. Each card holds one flat shape drawn as a teal outline inside a white circle, and beside it three name chips to choose from: circle, square, triangle or rectangle. The child names the shape and circles its word. The sheet shown runs a long, thin triangle lying almost on its side, a plain circle, a square tilted a few degrees, a rectangle turned on a slant, a square standing on one corner, and a tall narrow triangle. Only one of the six sits the way shapes usually sit in a picture book.
K-368.p2: That is the point of the page, and the instruction says so out loud: even the turned and skinny ones. Young children learn shape names from a small set of perfect examples, a triangle with a flat base and a square with its sides straight up and down, and then refuse to call a square on its corner a square. Every card here breaks one of those habits, so the name has to come from the sides and corners rather than from the pose. Card five is the one to talk about: most children will want to call it a diamond, and that word is not offered.
K-368.p3: One sheet, six shapes, six circles. This is the base page of the 2D shapes family and the one that owns the plain naming task; the five faces built on it ask the child to reject shapes that are not the real thing, find shapes in everyday objects, write the names, solve riddles, or draw shapes on dot paper. Each card has exactly one right chip, so the page checks quickly. If card five causes an argument, let it: turning the sheet until the square sits flat settles it in a second.

G1-381.title: 2D Shapes Real or Not Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-381.metaDescription: 2D shapes worksheet: three rows, each a shape name and four drawings. Circle every one that really is that shape; curves, gaps and rounded corners do not count.
G1-381.p1: Three wide rows make up this 1st grade page, each headed by one shape name in a teal pill and followed by four drawings in white circles. The child reads the name and circles every drawing that really is that shape, which can be more than one. On the sheet shown the triangle row holds three true triangles, all turned or stretched, and one shape with a curved side. The rectangle row has one upright rectangle beside a slanted four-sided shape, a rectangle with a gap in its outline and a tall shape with rounded corners. The square row pairs a small square and a tilted square with an unclosed square and a leaning rhombus.
G1-381.p2: This face turns the naming task around. Instead of choosing a word for a drawing, the child holds the word fixed and tests each drawing against it, which is how first graders learn to tell defining attributes from ones that do not matter: closed or open, straight sides or curved, square corners or not. Size and turning never decide anything here, and the rows are built so that they cannot. The near misses are the teaching: an outline with a small gap, a rectangle whose corners have been rounded off, a square pushed over into a rhombus.
G1-381.p3: One sheet, three rows, twelve drawings. The number of true shapes changes from row to row, so a child cannot simply circle one per row and stop; ask them to say why each rejected drawing fails before they move on. Use it after the base page, where every drawing was a real shape, and before the riddles face, which describes the same attributes in words instead of showing them.

K-371.title: 2D Shapes Around Us Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free PDF
K-371.metaDescription: 2D shapes around us worksheet: eight everyday pictures, each with a circle and a rectangle to color. Envelope, plate, lollipop, door, clock, map, board, pizza.
K-371.p1: Eight picture cards fill this kindergarten page in two columns. Each shows a familiar object in color on the left and, on the right, two outline tiles: a circle labeled circle and a rectangle labeled rectangle. The child decides which shape the object has and colors that tile. The sheet shown runs an envelope, a plate, a lollipop, a door, a wall clock, a wall map hanging from a rod, a whiteboard and a pizza, four round things and four rectangular ones, mixed so that no long run of one answer builds up down the page.
K-371.p2: This face takes the shape names off the page and into the room. The objects are chosen because each has one flat face a young child can see as a circle or a rectangle without thinking about depth: the round rim of a plate, the front of a door, the sheet of a wall map. That is the kindergarten expectation of naming shapes in the world around us, and it is why only two shapes are offered; the question is which of two, not which of four. The lollipop is the card most likely to stop someone, because the stick is a line and only the candy is round.
K-371.p3: One sheet, eight pictures, eight colored tiles. Coloring rather than circling makes it slower and calmer than the other faces, which suits a first shape lesson. Afterwards, send the class to find three round things and three rectangular things in the classroom and name them aloud. Every rectangular object on the page has sharp square corners, so nothing here contradicts the Real or Not face, where a rectangle with rounded corners is ruled out.

G1-382.title: 2D Shapes Names Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-382.metaDescription: 2D shape names worksheet: six shapes, each beside a handwriting line, and a box with circle, square, triangle and rectangle to copy from. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-382.p1: Six long rows run down this 1st grade page, each with one shape in a white circle on the left and a three-line handwriting lane beside it. A dashed box across the top holds the four names to copy from: rectangle, triangle, square and circle. On the sheet shown the shapes are a tilted rectangle, a circle, a tilted square, a thin triangle leaning to one side, a flat rectangle and an upright square, so rectangle and square each appear twice and two of the six are turned.
G1-382.p2: Writing a name is a harder retrieval than circling one. On the base page the right word was one of three chips; here the child has to know which word goes with the drawing, find it in the box and copy it letter by letter onto a ruled line, and all four names are in play for every row. That makes it a first grade production page for a kindergarten naming skill, and it is honest about that: it reviews the names rather than adding a new idea. The two tilted four-sided shapes are where the thinking happens, since telling the square from the rectangle depends on the side lengths, not the angle.
G1-382.p3: One sheet, six shapes, six written names. The word box stays on the page, so spelling is supported but not given away. If a child writes the right name with a reversed letter, the shape knowledge is there and the handwriting is a separate conversation. This face pairs well with the riddles face, which asks for the same four names from a description instead of a drawing.

G1-383.title: 2D Shape Riddles Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-383.metaDescription: 2D shape riddles worksheet: five What am I? riddles about sides and corners, one each for circle, square, triangle, hexagon and rectangle. Circle the name. 1st grade PDF.
G1-383.p1: Five riddle cards fill this 1st grade page, four in two columns and a wide one across the bottom, each with a question mark in its corner, a short riddle in a pale bubble and three name chips underneath. The child reads the riddle and circles the shape it describes. The riddles are written in the shape's own voice and never use its name: I am round all the way around and have no corners. All my 4 sides are the same length, and my corners are like a book corner. I have 3 sides and 3 corners. I have 6 sides and 6 corners. My 4 corners are like a book corner, and I have 2 long and 2 short sides. Each of the five shapes gets exactly one riddle, and the hexagon is the new name on this face.
G1-383.p2: Riddles move shape knowledge from seeing to describing. A child who can pick out a triangle may still not be able to say that it has three sides, and this page asks them to go the other way, from the attribute to the name, which is the first grade work of describing shapes by the features that define them. The book corner is the page's word for a right angle, chosen because every child has one within reach. The rectangle riddle offers square as one of its choices, so the book corners alone do not settle it: the child has to read that there are two long and two short sides. The square riddle keeps rectangle off its chips, since a square is a rectangle too and both names would be true.
G1-383.p3: One sheet, five riddles, five circles. The reading load is real, so read the riddles aloud with children who are still decoding; the shape thinking is the point, not the reading. For a stretch, cover the chips and ask for the name without a choice, or ask a child to write a sixth riddle for a shape of their own. The write-the-names face and this one share the core names, and doing both in a week gives the vocabulary two different routes in.

K-372.title: Draw 2D Shapes on Dot Paper, Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-372.metaDescription: Draw 2D shapes on dot paper: four 6-by-6 dot grids, each headed by a shape name. Join the dots to draw a triangle, two squares and a rectangle. Kindergarten PDF.
K-372.p1: Four large panels share this kindergarten page, each a six-by-six grid of dots under a shape name in a teal pill. The child reads the name and joins the dots with straight lines to draw that shape. On the sheet shown the panels ask for a triangle, a square, a second square and a rectangle. The first two grids are empty, so the child chooses where to start and how big to make the shape. The second square begins from one thick orange side already drawn straight across, three spaces long, and the rectangle from a thick orange side standing straight up, four spaces tall.
K-372.p2: Drawing a shape is the kindergarten step after naming it, and dot paper makes it possible for small hands: the dots do the measuring, so straight sides and square corners come from counting along a row instead of from a steady ruler. The open panels let a child draw any size they like. The given sides add one small condition. To finish the square, the child counts the three spaces along the orange line and then goes down three spaces, so all four sides match. To finish the rectangle, the other side has to be a different length from the four-space side, which is the whole difference between the two shapes.
K-372.p3: One sheet, four grids, four drawn shapes. Pencils work better than crayons on dot paper, and a finger walk along the dots before drawing helps children see the side lengths. Every given side runs along the grid, straight across or straight up, so no panel asks a five-year-old to draw a tilted shape. The base page and the real-or-not face both show turned shapes to recognize; this is the face where the child makes a shape of their own.

K-369.h1: Road Safety: Read the Traffic Light
K-369.title: Road Safety Worksheet for Kindergarten: Traffic Light | Free PDF
K-369.metaDescription: Road safety worksheet: six signal scenes, three for cars and three for walkers. Find the lamp that is on and circle stop or go, wait or walk. Kindergarten PDF.
K-369.p1: Six scenes fill this kindergarten page, each built around one signal on a pole above a strip of road. Three are car signals with three round lamps and a car on either side, one parked and one moving, under the chips stop and go. The other three are walking signals with a raised hand on top and a walking figure below, under the chips wait and walk, with a standing person and a striding person beside them. In every scene one lamp is lit and has short rays around it, and the two chips swap sides from one scene to the next, so the answer is never always on the same side. On the sheet shown the car signals show red, red and green, and the walking signals show the orange hand once and the white walking figure twice.
K-369.p2: Reading a signal is the first road safety skill a young child can practice on paper, and the page keeps it to exactly that: find the lamp that is on, then decide what it tells you to do. Car lights and walking lights are mixed on purpose, because children cross at both and the two use different words. The yellow lamp is never lit on this page, since slowing down is not a choice a child on foot makes. The walking signals follow the United States pattern, with the raised hand and the walking figure used at American crosswalks.
K-369.p3: One sheet, six signals, six circles. There is no Common Core standard for road safety; this is kindergarten to grade 2 pedestrian education, usually taught at the start of the school year or before a walking trip. Read the page aloud and act it out: stand at a pretend curb and have the class stop or walk as you point to each scene. The coloring face turns the same three lamps into a coloring task, and the crossing steps face puts the whole routine in order.

K-373.h1: Road Safety: Color the Traffic Lights
K-373.title: Traffic Light Coloring Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free PDF
K-373.metaDescription: Traffic light coloring worksheet: six blank signals, one lamp on each marked with rays. Color it red, yellow or green by where it sits. Kindergarten road safety PDF.
K-373.p1: Six blank traffic lights stand in two rows on this kindergarten page, each a tall three-lamp signal on a pole with a strip of road beneath. None of the lamps is colored in. On each signal one lamp has short rays drawn around it, and the child's job is to color that lamp the color it shines. On the sheet shown the rays sit on the top lamp twice, the middle lamp twice and the bottom lamp twice, so the finished page shows two red lights, two yellow and two green.
K-373.p2: There is no color on the page to copy, which is the whole idea. A child can only pick the right crayon by knowing that the top lamp is red, the middle one yellow and the bottom one green, so the page checks the order of the lamps rather than the meaning of the colors. That order is what lets people read a signal from far away or in bright sun, and it is what a child who cannot easily tell red from green relies on. Talk about what each color tells drivers to do once the coloring is finished.
K-373.p3: One sheet, six signals, six lamps to color. Have red, yellow and green crayons out before starting, and ask children to point to the rays before they pick a color. It is the calmest page in the road safety family and works as a first lesson or a quiet follow-up to the base page, where the signals are already lit and the child decides between stop and go, wait and walk. Pin the finished sheets up by the classroom door before a walking trip.

K-374.h1: Crossing the Road Safely: the Steps
K-374.title: Crossing the Road Safely Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free PDF
K-374.metaDescription: Crossing the road safely worksheet: four shuffled cards of a child at a crosswalk. Write 1 to 4 to order stop, look left, look right and walk when it is clear.
K-374.p1: Four picture cards sit on this kindergarten page in two rows of two, each with a dashed box underneath for a number. Every card shows the same child seen from behind, wearing a backpack, at the edge of a striped crosswalk. What changes is the child's action: standing still at the curb, looking left with an arrow, looking right with an arrow, and walking forward across the stripes. There are no cars on any card, so the road is clear when the child walks. The cards are mixed up, and the child writes 1 to 4 in the boxes to put the crossing in order.
K-374.p2: The routine on this page is stop at the curb, look left, look right, then walk when the road is clear, and children have to hold the whole routine in their heads rather than recognize one part of it. Showing the child from behind matters, because then left on the page is the child's own left, and the arrows point the way the head turns. The standing card is the one to talk about first: stopping is a step of its own, not just the moment before looking, and it is the step young children most often skip. Ask children to explain their order before marking it.
K-374.p3: One sheet, four cards, four numbers. Act the sequence out in the classroom or on the playground before or after the page; saying the steps aloud while turning the head is how the routine sticks. Many families also teach a second look left just before stepping off, which is worth adding aloud. This is the most practical face in the road safety family and the one to send home before a walking trip. The base page covers traffic and walking signals, which is the step that comes before this one at a light.

G1-384.h1: Road Safety: Traffic Signs and Their Meanings
G1-384.title: Traffic Signs and Their Meanings Worksheet, 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-384.metaDescription: Traffic signs worksheet: match six US road signs to what they mean. School zone, crosswalk, STOP, signal ahead, YIELD and DO NOT ENTER. 1st grade road safety PDF.
G1-384.p1: Six US road signs run down the left side of this 1st grade page, each in its own box with a dot beside it, and six short meanings run down the right. The child draws a line from each sign to what it means. The sheet shown matches a yellow five-sided school sign with two children on it, a yellow diamond with a walking person, a red octagon reading STOP, a yellow diamond with a traffic signal, a red and white triangle reading YIELD, and a round red DO NOT ENTER sign. The meanings are written in a child's words, such as A school is near, so look out for children and Every car must halt here, then look.
G1-384.p2: Signs are how the road talks to people, and a first grader can learn to read them by shape and color before reading every word on them. This page teaches the signs a child meets on the way to school, all drawn to the United States sign standards, so the octagon, the diamond and the five-sided school sign look as they do on American streets. Each meaning fits only one sign: the school sign warns that a school is near, while the walking diamond marks a place where people cross the road, so point out the schoolhouse outline before matching.
G1-384.p3: One sheet, six signs, six lines. Take the page on a walk around the school block and tick off any sign you see; most neighborhoods have at least three of these six. The sorting face asks which signs give a rule and which give a warning, and the quiz face turns the meanings into sentences with three signs to choose from, so this page is the one to start with.

G2-360.h1: Road Safety: Kinds of Traffic Signs
G2-360.title: Kinds of Traffic Signs Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-360.metaDescription: Kinds of traffic signs worksheet: eight lettered US signs to sort into rule signs and warning signs, four boxes each. Write the letters. 2nd grade road safety PDF.
G2-360.p1: Eight lettered road signs fill the top of this 2nd grade page in two rows, each on its own post, and two sorting panels sit at the bottom, Rule signs and Warning signs, with four dashed boxes each. The child writes the letter of every sign into the boxes of its group. The sheet shown mixes a no bicycles sign and a no walking sign, both white squares with a red circle and slash, the YIELD triangle and the STOP octagon with four yellow warnings: a walking person, a traffic signal, a bicycle and the five-sided school sign.
G2-360.p2: Sorting signs by kind is where road safety starts to become a system rather than a list. Rule signs tell you what you must or must not do and are mostly red and white; warning signs tell you what is ahead and are yellow, usually diamonds. A second grader who has learned that pattern can make a sensible guess about a sign they have never seen. The page pairs signs that share a picture across the two groups, a walking person as a warning and a crossed-out walking person as a rule, so color and shape have to carry the decision rather than the picture.
G2-360.p3: One sheet, eight signs, eight letters. Both panels have exactly four boxes, which tells children how many belong in each group; if you want the sort to be harder, have them list the letters on a separate strip instead. Afterwards, ask them to invent a sign for the classroom and decide which group it belongs in. The quiz face comes after this one and uses the same sign table.

G2-361.h1: Road Safety Quiz: Which Sign Fits?
G2-361.title: Road Sign Quiz Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-361.metaDescription: Road sign quiz worksheet: six sentences about the road, each beside three US signs. Circle the one sign that fits, from the school sign to DO NOT ENTER. 2nd grade PDF.
G2-361.p1: Six sentence cards run down the left of this 2nd grade page, each with three road signs lined up beside it. The child reads the sentence and circles the one sign that fits. The sentences describe a situation rather than a sign: Drivers go slowly because kids are going to and from class. This is a spot where people cross the road on foot. There is a traffic light a little way down this road. Bicycles are not allowed here. Push yours on another path. Slow down and let the cars on the big road go first. This is the wrong way in, so drivers must turn around.
G2-361.p2: This is the reading face of the road safety family and the one that tests understanding rather than recognition. Each row sets the right sign beside two that look possible, often a sign with the same picture: the no bicycles rule sits next to the bicycle warning, the walking warning next to the no walking rule. A child who matches by the picture alone will get those rows wrong; one who reads the sentence and asks whether it is a rule or a warning will get them right. The right answer moves between the three positions from row to row.
G2-361.p3: One sheet, six sentences, six circles. The sentences are long for a second grader, so pair readers or read them aloud if the sign knowledge is what you want to check. Use it after the sorting face, which sets up the rule-or-warning idea it depends on. As a follow-up, ask children to write one sentence of their own for a sign on the page and swap with a partner.

K-370.title: Family Members Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-370.metaDescription: Family members worksheet: a three-generation family tree with five numbered people and a named child. Write each number beside sister, mom, grandma, grandpa, dad.
K-370.p1: A small family tree fills the top half of this kindergarten page: two grandparents at the top, two parents in the middle and two children at the bottom, each drawn as a simple portrait in a frame and joined by lines. One child is marked with an orange star and named, Eli on the sheet shown. The other five people carry numbers from 1 to 5. Below the tree sit five family word chips, sister, mom, grandma, grandpa and dad, each with a dashed box. The child finds each person on the tree and writes their number next to the right word.
K-370.p2: Every family word depends on who is speaking, and the star is what makes the page work: the words are all Eli's. The girl next to him is his sister, drawn a little taller because she is the older child, and the grandparents are his dad's parents, because the line from the top joins them to his dad, not his mom. A kindergartner does not need to explain that, but following the lines to find it is the beginning of reading a family tree. The portraits are simple on purpose, with glasses and gray hair for the grandparents, so children look at where people sit on the tree as well as how they look.
K-370.p3: One sheet, one tree, five numbers. This is kindergarten to grade 2 social studies readiness; there is no Common Core standard for family words. Afterwards, ask children to draw their own family on the back and point to one person for each word they used. The trace-and-write face uses the same kind of tree with the words printed to trace, and the family tree template lets children draw their own people in the frames.

G1-385.title: Family Generations Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-385.metaDescription: Family generations worksheet: six rows of three family words. Write 1, 2 and 3 to order them from the oldest generation to the youngest, with a picture key on top.
G1-385.p1: A picture key runs across the top of this 1st grade page: three framed pairs of people hanging from one line and numbered 1, 2 and 3, grandparents first, then parents, then children. Below it are six rows, each holding three family words with a dashed box beside each one. The child writes 1, 2 and 3 to put the three words in order from the oldest generation to the youngest. The sheet shown mixes grandma, grandpa, mom, dad, uncle, aunt, sister, brother, cousin, baby sister and baby brother; the first row, for instance, is sister, grandma and uncle.
G1-385.p2: The question here is not who is older but which generation someone belongs to, and that is a first grade idea worth separating out. An uncle may be younger than a mom, and a cousin can be a grown-up, but on a family tree the uncle sits with the parents and the cousin with the children. The key at the top gives the three levels, so the child can place each word before comparing. Aunts, uncles and cousins appear alongside the core family words so the child has to think about the shape of a whole family, not just its closest members.
G1-385.p3: One sheet, six rows, eighteen numbers. Every row uses all three generations exactly once, so a row where two words seem to share a level is a sign to look again at the key. It follows the Who Is Who? base page, which introduced the tree, and comes before the clues face, where children fill in a whole tree from written sentences.

K-375.title: Family Words Trace and Write, Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-375.metaDescription: Family words tracing worksheet: a family tree with five numbered people and a named child. Trace grandpa, grandma, brother, mom and dad, then write each again.
K-375.p1: A family tree sits on the left of this kindergarten page: two grandparents at the top, two parents below them and two children at the bottom, one of them starred and named Anna on the sheet shown. The other five people carry the numbers 1 to 5. On the right, a panel holds five family words in dotted letters to trace, grandpa, grandma, brother, mom and dad, each with a number beside it that matches a person on the tree. Below the panel are five writing lines numbered 1 to 5. The child finds the person with each number, traces their family word and writes it again on the line with the same number.
K-375.p2: This face joins the family words to the letters that spell them. Kindergarten children use mom and dad as spoken words long before they read them, and tracing each word beside its number links the sound, the spelling and the person on the tree. The traced words are not listed in number order while the writing lines are, so the child has to look back at the tree and the numbers for every line, and the page stays about the family, not only about handwriting. The words are Anna's: the grandparents are joined to her mom by the tree line, which is worth pointing out.
K-375.p3: One sheet, five words to trace, five to write. The dotted letters are large and use a plain printed alphabet, so this page sits comfortably alongside any handwriting program. The grandpa has curly gray hair and a mustache and the grandma wears glasses, so the two are easy to tell apart at the top of the tree. Use it after the Who Is Who? base page, once the words are familiar. The generations face at first grade adds aunts, uncles and cousins.

G1-386.title: Family Tree Worksheet for 1st Grade: Read the Clues | Free PDF
G1-386.metaDescription: Family tree worksheet: a three-generation tree with three names given and four empty name boxes. Read four clues like Anna is Jack's mom and write each name in place.
G1-386.p1: A three-generation family tree fills most of this 1st grade page. There are seven people, each in a portrait frame with a name box underneath: two grandparents at the top, two sisters in the middle with one sister's husband beside her, and two brothers at the bottom. Three name boxes are already filled, Mia, Ben and Jack on the sheet shown, and Jack is marked with a star. The other four boxes are empty. Below the tree four numbered clues give the missing names: Leo is Jack's brother. Anna is Jack's mom. Eli is Jack's grandpa. Ava is Jack's aunt.
G1-386.p2: This is the reasoning face of the family: the child has to read a relationship and then find where that relationship sits on the tree. The aunt and the mom are both women in the middle row, and only the tree lines tell them apart, since Jack's mom is the one joined to Ben and to the children. Every clue is written from Jack's side, which is how family trees are usually read, and the given names act as anchors so no clue has to be solved blind.
G1-386.p3: One sheet, four clues, four names to write. Read the clues aloud with early readers and let them do the tree work themselves, and encourage children to cross out a clue once its name is placed. If a child puts Anna and Ava the wrong way round, ask which woman is joined to Jack by a line; that is usually enough. The relationship riddles face takes the same thinking further without any pictures.

G2-362.title: Family Relationship Riddles Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-362.metaDescription: Family relationships worksheet: eight riddles like Tom's dad's mom is Tom's ... Write the family word from a box of four: grandpa, uncle, grandma, aunt.
G2-362.p1: A starred portrait of a boy named Tom sits at the top left of this 2nd grade page, beside a word box holding four family words: grandpa, uncle, grandma and aunt. Below are eight numbered riddles, each one sentence ending in a blank, such as Tom's dad's mom is Tom's ... and Tom's mom's brother is Tom's .... The child writes the right family word on each line. The instruction says outright that one word can fit more than one riddle, and on the sheet shown every word in the box answers exactly two, one from his mom's side and one from his dad's.
G2-362.p2: The riddles ask children to put two relationships together into one, which is the thinking behind reading any family tree: a mom's mom is a grandma, a dad's sister is an aunt. Both sides of the family appear, so the child meets the fact that Tom has two grandmas and that the word does not change with the side. Every word in the box is an answer, so the challenge is not ruling out distractors but seeing that two different paths lead to the same word; a child who looks for eight different answers will stop and ask.
G2-362.p3: One sheet, eight riddles, eight words. There is no tree to lean on, so draw one on the board for children who need it and let them point along the lines. Second graders enjoy writing a riddle of their own in the same pattern for a classmate to solve. This page builds on the clues face, which solved the same kind of relationship with pictures, and the family tree template is a good way to finish the unit.

G1-387.title: Family Tree Template for Kids, 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-387.metaDescription: Family tree template for kids: an open tree with a me frame at the trunk, nine frames on the branches and four on a shelf, each with a name line. 1st grade PDF.
G1-387.p1: This 1st grade page is an open family tree for a child to fill in. A frame labeled me sits at the foot of the trunk, with its own short line for the child's name. Three frames hang from the top branches, four from the wide middle branch and two from the low branch on either side of the trunk, and four more stand on a shelf below the tree, fourteen frames in all, in circles, squares and arches. Every frame has a ruled line underneath or beside it for a name. The instruction asks children to draw the people who are important to them in the frames and write their names on the lines.
G1-387.p2: There is nothing to get right on this page, and that is deliberate. The tree is not labeled with grandparents or parents, so a child with one parent, two moms, a grandparent at home, stepbrothers or a family spread across countries can fill it honestly without leaving a box labeled for someone who is not there. The shelf at the bottom holds people and pets who matter but do not fit on the branches. Children decide where each person goes, and that choice is often the best part of the conversation.
G1-387.p3: One sheet, fourteen frames, fourteen name lines. Send it home as a family project or use it at the end of a family unit, after the pages that teach the words. Not every frame needs filling; tell children that before they start. The drawings are small, so colored pencils work better than crayons. The Who Is Who? and clues faces are the pages that teach the family words this one leaves open.

G1-376.title: Parts of a Plant Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-376.metaDescription: Parts of a plant worksheet: a flowering plant with six numbered tags and a word bank of roots, stem, leaf, flower, fruit and seed. Label the diagram. 1st grade PDF.
G1-376.p1: A tall flowering plant fills the left of this 1st grade page, growing from a box of soil with its roots drawn underground. It has a white flower at the top, four leaves up the stem and a green pod hanging from the side with four dark seeds inside. Six orange numbered tags point to parts of it with thin lines, each ending in a small ring. A word bank across the top holds six words, seed, leaf, stem, fruit, roots and flower, and six numbered lines on the right wait for the names. On the sheet shown tag 1 points to the roots, 3 to the stem, 4 to a petal of the flower and 6 to a leaf, while 2 and 5 both land on the pod.
G1-376.p2: Naming the parts is the first step in the first grade science idea that a plant's structures help it live and grow; a later face asks what each part does. The pod is the part to slow down on. It is the fruit of the plant, and the round things inside it are the seeds, so tag 2 rings the empty top end of the pod, above the seeds, and tag 5 rings one seed in the row. Ask children to say what each ring sits on before they write: the pod wall is the fruit, the dark ball is a seed.
G1-376.p3: One sheet, six tags, six names. Roots is plural and leaf singular because that is how the diagram shows them. A real plant on the windowsill makes the best companion, since children can find the same parts on it. This is the base page of the plants family; its faces cover what plants need, the seed-to-plant cycle, the parts we eat, the job of each part and the parts of a flower. In NGSS terms it supports 1-LS1-1.

K-376.title: What Plants Need to Grow Worksheet for Kindergarten | Free PDF
K-376.metaDescription: What plants need to grow worksheet: ten potted seedlings in five rows, each fed by two things. Circle the plant in each row that gets both sun and water. K science PDF.
K-376.p1: Ten small cards fill this kindergarten page in five rows of two. Every card shows the same seedling in a pot in the middle, with an arrow pointing in from each side and a picture at the end of each arrow. Some plants get a smiling sun and a drop of water. Others get only one of them, paired with something a plant does not need: a toy train, a green car, a toy robot or a glove. One plant on the sheet shown gets neither, just a shoe and a pencil. In each row the child circles the plant that gets both things it needs.
K-376.p2: Plants need light and water to grow, and kindergarten science asks children to notice that from what they see. This page turns the idea into a quick yes or no: look at the two arrows, check each picture, and only circle the plant that has both. The distractors are everyday objects, so the choice is never between two plant needs, only between a need and a thing. In every row exactly one plant has sun and water, and it sits sometimes on the left and sometimes on the right.
K-376.p3: One sheet, five rows, five circles. Each row sits in its own framed band with the two cards side by side, so point along the first band with the class before they start to show how the pairs work. Planting beans in two cups, one on the windowsill and one in a cupboard, turns the page into an experiment children remember. In NGSS terms it supports K-LS1-1. The seed-to-plant face shows what those needs make possible.

G1-388.h1: Plant Life Cycle: From Seed to Plant
G1-388.title: Plant Life Cycle Cut and Paste Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-388.metaDescription: Plant life cycle worksheet: a seed in soil and four empty boxes round a loop of arrows. Cut out four stages and glue them in order, sprout to pod. 1st grade PDF.
G1-388.p1: A seed lying in a box of soil sits at the top of this 1st grade page, and four empty dashed boxes circle down and round from it, linked by curved arrows that lead back to the seed. Across the bottom is a strip of four pictures to cut out along dashed lines, marked with a pair of scissors. The four pictures come mixed up: a seed splitting with a root and a shoot coming out, a small seedling with two leaves, a flowering plant and a plant carrying a pea pod. The child cuts them out and glues each one in the next empty box, going round the arrows from the seed.
G1-388.p2: The order is the lesson: seed, sprouting seed, seedling, flowering plant, plant with a pod, and back to seeds. Every picture uses the same box of soil, so the only thing that changes from stage to stage is the plant, and children can see the roots grow along with the shoot. The loop matters as much as the order. Arrows running back to the start show that the pod holds new seeds, which is what makes it a cycle rather than a story that ends with a flower.
G1-388.p3: One sheet, five stages, four to glue. Cutting and gluing takes longer than writing numbers, so allow a full lesson and have glue sticks ready; children who finish early can write one word under each stage. This face sits between the base diagram, which names the parts, and the parts we eat, and it pairs naturally with the butterfly and frog pages in the animal life cycles family. In NGSS it touches 3-LS1-1, brought down here to a simple first grade sequence.

G2-363.h1: Parts of a Plant We Eat
G2-363.title: Parts of a Plant We Eat Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-363.metaDescription: Parts of a plant we eat worksheet: eight vegetables, each with three part names to circle. Celery, radish, corn, lettuce, carrot, eggplant, cauliflower, spinach.
G2-363.p1: Eight food cards fill this 2nd grade page in two columns. Each shows a vegetable in color on the left and three part chips on the right, every chip with a small icon: seed, flower, roots, stem, leaf or fruit. The child circles the part of the plant that we eat. The sheet shown runs a stick of celery, a radish, an ear of corn in its husk, a head of lettuce, a carrot, an eggplant, a cauliflower and a spinach leaf, so roots and leaves come up twice each and stem, seed, fruit and flower once each.
G2-363.p2: Most children know these foods and have never thought of them as plant parts. Circling the part turns a lunchbox into a science lesson: the carrot is a root, celery is a stem, the cauliflower is a head of flowers that have not opened yet. The eggplant is the card to talk about, because in the kitchen it is a vegetable and on the plant it is a fruit, the part that holds the seeds. The corn card asks for the kernels, the seeds we eat, and its chips offer seed, stem and roots, so the husk around it does not muddy the choice.
G2-363.p3: One sheet, eight foods, eight circles. The icons repeat the shapes from the base diagram, so children who have done that page have a visual reminder of each part. Bring in a few real vegetables and sort them by part as a class; roots and leaves are easy to find, flowers less so. The functions face, which asks what each part does, is the natural next step, and the base page is the one to do first.

G2-364.h1: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
G2-364.title: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions Worksheet, 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-364.metaDescription: Parts of a plant and their functions worksheet: a tagged plant diagram and five jobs, like makes food from sunlight. Write the tag number of each part. 2nd grade PDF.
G2-364.p1: The same flowering plant as the base page stands on the left of this 2nd grade page, this time with five orange numbered tags: 1 on the stem, 2 on a seed inside the pod, 3 on the flower, 4 on a leaf and 5 on the roots. On the right, five jobs are written in plain words, each with a dashed box: can grow into a new plant; makes food for the plant from sunlight; takes in water from the soil; holds the plant up tall; calls bees to come and visit it. The child finds the part that does each job and writes its tag number in the box.
G2-364.p2: This is the step from naming to explaining. Knowing that a leaf is called a leaf is not the same as knowing it makes the plant's food, and second graders are ready to link each structure to what it does. The jobs are written without any part names, so the child has to reason from the description to the diagram. Pollination appears in its simplest form, a flower calling bees to visit, which sets up the flower face at grade 3; ask children how a flower might call a bee, and color and scent will come up on their own.
G2-364.p3: One sheet, five jobs, five numbers. It is shorter than the base page and more demanding, so give it once the parts are secure. A good follow-up is to act the jobs out: roots drink, the stem stands tall, leaves reach for the sun. The parts of a flower face zooms in on the one part this page treats as a whole. In NGSS terms this reaches toward 4-LS1-1, so it is a stretch for many second grade classes.

G3-392.title: Parts of a Flower Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-392.metaDescription: Parts of a flower worksheet: a close-up flower with four numbered parts and a bank of sepal, stamen, roots, petal and pistil. Name each; cross out the odd word.
G3-392.p1: A large close-up of one flower fills the middle of this 3rd grade page, opened out so the inside shows: long petals, dark-tipped stamens around a central pistil and green sepals at the base, all on a stem. A small inset on the right shows the plant it comes from, stem and leaves with no roots drawn, and the flower circled, so children can see where the close-up comes from. Four numbered tags point to parts: 1 a sepal, 2 a stamen, 3 the pistil and 4 a petal. A bank at the top holds five words, the four flower parts and roots, and four numbered lines wait below. The child writes each part's name and crosses out the word that is not a part of a flower.
G3-392.p2: The flower is where a plant makes its seeds, and naming the pistil and stamen is the vocabulary children need before they can talk about pollination. Roots is the intruder in the bank, a real plant part that belongs to a different diagram, so crossing it out checks that children know where the flower ends. With four tags and four flower words, the bank leaves no spare flower word to guess with: a child who mixes up the pistil and a stamen will find two words fighting for one line.
G3-392.p3: One sheet, four parts, one word crossed out. This page sits above the kindergarten to grade 2 range of the rest of the plants family; flower structure usually arrives in grade 3 or 4, and in NGSS it belongs with 4-LS1-1. A real tulip or lily cut in half lets children find every part with a magnifying glass. The base diagram and the functions face are the right pages to do first.

G1-377.title: Butterfly Life Cycle Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-377.metaDescription: Butterfly life cycle worksheet: four magnified circles round a plant, egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly. The egg is 1; number the rest and close the cycle.
G1-377.p1: A tall plant grows up the middle of this 1st grade page, and four big circles around it act like magnifying glasses, each joined by a line to a small spot on the plant. One shows a ridged egg on a leaf, one a caterpillar on a leaf, one a chrysalis hanging under a leaf and one an orange butterfly on the flower. The egg is already marked 1. The child writes 2, 3 and 4 in the dashed boxes under the other three as the butterfly grows. Below a dotted line the butterfly appears again with a looping arrow and one last box, and there the child writes the number of the picture that comes after the butterfly.
G1-377.p2: That last box is what turns a sequence into a cycle. The answer is 1, because the butterfly lays the egg, and a child who writes 5 has shown that they still think of the life cycle as a line with an end. The four stages sit where they really happen on a plant, the egg on a leaf and the chrysalis hanging underneath one, so the page also shows that every stage lives on the same plant. The word chrysalis is used rather than cocoon, which belongs to a moth.
G1-377.p3: One sheet, four stages, four numbers. This is the base page of the animal life cycles family; its faces add the frog, the labeling words, metamorphosis across three animals, a comparison and a what-comes-next page. The full cycle belongs to grade 3 in NGSS, as 3-LS1-1, and this page brings it down to a first grade numbering task. Raising caterpillars in the classroom in spring is the best companion if you can manage it.

G1-389.h1: Frog Life Cycle: Cut and Paste
G1-389.title: Frog Life Cycle Cut and Paste Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-389.metaDescription: Frog life cycle cut and paste worksheet: frogspawn on the top lily pad and four empty pads round a pond. Cut out tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet and frog.
G1-389.p1: A round pond fills most of this 1st grade page, with five white lily pads around its edge joined by orange arrows. The top pad already shows a clump of frogspawn in the water, and the other four pads each hold an empty dashed square. At the bottom is a strip of four round pictures to cut out, in mixed order: a plain tadpole, a tadpole with back legs, a small froglet on a lily pad and a grown frog on a lily pad. The child cuts out the four squares and glues each one on its pad, going round the pond from the frogspawn to the frog.
G1-389.p2: The frog's cycle is the one children find most surprising, because the young animal lives in water, breathes differently and looks nothing like its parent. Frogspawn, tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet and frog is the order a first grader can learn, and the arrows run back from the frog to the frogspawn so the cycle closes. The froglet and the frog both sit on a lily pad, but the froglet is smaller and still has a short tail, so ask children to look for the tail before they glue.
G1-389.p3: One sheet, five stages, four to glue. Scissors and glue make this a longer lesson than the base page, and it rewards a short talk first about what a tadpole eats and where it lives. It pairs with the plant cut and paste page in the plants family, which uses the same loop of boxes. In NGSS terms it supports 3-LS1-1 early. The compare face at grade 3 puts this cycle side by side with the butterfly.

G2-365.title: Label the Butterfly Life Cycle Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-365.metaDescription: Label the butterfly life cycle worksheet: four stages in a loop of arrows and a bank of egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly and tadpole. Cross out the odd one.
G2-365.p1: Four large circles sit in a square on this 2nd grade page, linked by orange arrows that run clockwise: an egg on a leaf top left, a caterpillar on a leaf top right, a chrysalis hanging from a leaf bottom right and a butterfly bottom left, with the last arrow running back up to the egg. Each picture has a ruled line underneath. A word bank at the top holds five names in mixed order: the four stage names egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and butterfly, plus tadpole. The child writes each name on the line under its picture and crosses out the one name that does not belong.
G2-365.p2: Writing the stage names is the grade 2 step after numbering them on the base page. The pictures are already in order, so the task is vocabulary: can the child connect caterpillar and chrysalis to the right drawings and spell them from the bank? Tadpole is the intruder. It is a real life-cycle word and a very likely wrong answer for a child who has just done the frog page, which is exactly why it is here. Crossing it out is a quick check that the two cycles are not being blended.
G2-365.p3: One sheet, four labels, one word crossed out. Spelling chrysalis is hard; the bank gives it, and that is enough at this grade. Use it after the base page and the frog cut and paste, and before the metamorphosis face, where children sort young animals into three cycles at once. A classroom chart with the four words and the loop of arrows makes a good anchor for the week.

G2-366.h1: Metamorphosis: Which Animal Will It Become?
G2-366.title: Metamorphosis Worksheet, 2nd Grade: Butterfly, Frog, Ladybug | Free PDF
G2-366.metaDescription: Metamorphosis worksheet: eight life-cycle stages lettered A to H to sort under the butterfly, the frog and the ladybug they will become. Free 2nd grade science PDF.
G2-366.p1: Eight lettered circles fill the top of this 2nd grade page, each showing an early stage of an animal. Below stand three tall panels headed by grown-up animals, a butterfly, a frog and a ladybug, each with four dashed boxes inside for letters. The child looks at each stage and writes its letter in a box under the grown-up it will become, and the instruction warns that some boxes stay empty. The sheet shown mixes a chrysalis, a ladybug pupa, a tadpole with legs, a ladybug larva, a clump of frogspawn, a froglet, a caterpillar and a tadpole.
G2-366.p2: Metamorphosis means the young look nothing like the adult, and this page makes that the whole puzzle. A ladybug larva is long, dark and spiky and does not resemble a ladybug at all; a caterpillar does not resemble a butterfly. The child has to know the cycles well enough to trace backwards from the adult. Three animals rather than two stop children from sorting by elimination. The stages include eggs and resting pupae as well as young animals, frogspawn and a chrysalis among them, so name each stage properly as you go.
G2-366.p3: One sheet, eight stages, eight letters. Every panel has four boxes, so the boxes no longer tell children how many letters belong to each animal: on the sheet shown the frog takes four and the butterfly and ladybug two each. The ladybug is the new animal here and the one most children will need help with; a photo of a real ladybug larva on a rose leaf is convincing. This face supports NGSS 3-LS1-1 and, for how young animals come to look like their parents, 1-LS3-1.

G3-393.h1: Butterfly and Frog Life Cycles Compared
G3-393.title: Compare Butterfly and Frog Life Cycles, 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-393.metaDescription: Compare butterfly and frog life cycles: eight statements to check under the butterfly, the frog or both. Eggs, tails, six legs, nectar, chrysalis. 3rd grade PDF.
G3-393.p1: A butterfly and a frog head two columns at the top right of this 3rd grade page, and eight statements run down the left, each with a check box under each animal. The child reads a sentence and checks the butterfly, the frog or both when it is true for that animal. The statements on the sheet shown are: The grown-up catches insects to eat. The grown-up has six legs. It hatches from an egg. Its young has no legs at first. The grown-up drinks nectar from flowers. Its young swims with a tail. Its young looks very different from the grown-up. It spends one stage as a chrysalis.
G3-393.p2: Comparing two cycles is the grade 3 move, and it is where children stop learning a sequence and start learning a pattern. Both animals hatch from eggs and both change shape dramatically; only one has a pupa; only one starts life in water. Two statements are true for both animals and the rest for one, so there is no easy rule to guess by. The statement about legs is worth a pause: caterpillars do have legs, short ones near the head, so it is only the tadpole that begins without any.
G3-393.p3: One sheet, eight statements, ten checks in all. Ask children to explain one of the both answers aloud, since that is where the comparison really happens. This page supports NGSS 3-LS1-1, which asks students to see life cycles as a pattern of birth, growth, reproduction and death. It is the top of the animal life cycles family and follows the base butterfly page and the frog cut and paste naturally.

G1-390.h1: What Comes Next? Butterfly, Frog and Ladybug
G1-390.title: What Comes Next Life Cycle Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-390.metaDescription: What comes next life cycle worksheet: six rows, each a stage of a butterfly, frog or ladybug and three choices. Circle the stage that comes right after it. 1st grade.
G1-390.p1: Six rows fill this 1st grade page. Each begins with one life-cycle stage in a shaded frame, then an orange arrow, then three stages to choose from. The child looks at the first picture and circles the one that comes right after it. On the sheet shown the rows start from frogspawn, a chrysalis, a tadpole with legs, a grown ladybug, a butterfly and a clump of ladybug eggs, so all three animals appear twice and the choices in each row come from the same animal as the first picture.
G1-390.p2: Asking only for the next stage keeps the page short and makes the cycle idea sharp. Two rows start from a grown-up animal, the ladybug and the butterfly, and the right answer for each is its eggs, which is where the cycle begins again. Those two rows are the ones to watch: a child who circles nothing, or picks a baby animal, has not yet understood that adults lay eggs. Because every choice in a row comes from the same animal, the decision is always about order, never about which animal it is.
G1-390.p3: One sheet, six rows, six circles. Because all the pictures are stages of three animals, this page works as a review after the base butterfly page and the frog cut and paste. It is also the first time the ladybug appears at first grade, so a short look at its four stages first will help. The metamorphosis face at grade 2 uses the same ladybug pictures and asks the question the other way round.

G1-378.title: Sun, Earth and Moon Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-378.metaDescription: Sun, Earth and Moon worksheet: eight sentences to sort with a check under the Sun, the Earth or the Moon. Stars, craters, planets, day and night. 1st grade science PDF.
G1-378.p1: A three-column table fills this 1st grade page under pictures of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon, each labeled. Eight numbered sentences run down the left, each with a dashed box under all three, and the child puts a check under the one the sentence is true for. On the sheet shown the sentences are: It goes around our planet. Its turning gives us day and night. It is the biggest of the three. Its shape seems to change. It is a star. It is covered in craters. It is a planet. It is the hottest of the three.
G1-378.p2: The Sun, the Earth and the Moon are the three bodies first graders meet in science, and they often blend together: the Moon gives light, the Sun goes round us. Each sentence here gives one fact that belongs to only one of them, so the child has to keep the three apart. The patterns of the sky are the first grade idea, and this page gives children the facts to talk about them. The column pictures help a little: the Sun is drawn biggest and the Moon with craters, so ask children to explain an answer with a fact, not only by pointing at the picture.
G1-378.p3: One sheet, eight sentences, eight checks. On the sheet shown the Sun gets three sentences, the Moon three and the Earth two. This is the base page of the sun, moon and planets family; the faces go on to the moon phases, day and night, and the planets at grade 3. In NGSS it supports 1-ESS1-1. A flashlight and a ball in a dark room make the day and night sentence clear in a minute.

G1-391.title: Moon Phases in Order Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-391.metaDescription: Moon phases in order worksheet: two rows of five moons, one growing and one shrinking, with a wedge showing which. Write 1 to 5 under the moons. 1st grade PDF.
G1-391.p1: Two wide rows fill this 1st grade page, each holding five moons drawn as circles with their dark part shaded gray and their lit part left white, and a dashed box under each moon. Above each row is a wedge with an arrow: in the first row the wedge widens, meaning the Moon grows, and in the second it narrows, meaning it shrinks. The child writes 1 to 5 under the moons in that order. On the sheet shown the growing row runs from a new moon, all gray, through a thin crescent and a half moon to a nearly full moon and the full moon, and the shrinking row goes back down again.
G1-391.p2: The Moon's shape follows a pattern children can predict, and putting the phases in order is the first grade way to see it. The wedge is the page's key idea: it tells the child the direction before they start, so the task is ordering by how much is lit rather than remembering names. The lit side matters too. As seen from north of the equator, a growing moon is lit on the right and a shrinking one on the left, and the page draws them that way, so a sharp-eyed child can check an answer by the side.
G1-391.p3: One sheet, two rows, ten numbers. Phase names come later, on the name-the-moon-phases face; this page deliberately uses none. Keep a moon diary for a month alongside it, drawing the moon each clear evening, and compare the drawings with the rows. In NGSS it supports 1-ESS1-1. In the Southern Hemisphere the lit side is reversed, so tell traveling families that the pattern holds but the side flips.

G2-367.title: Name the Moon Phases Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-367.metaDescription: Name the moon phases worksheet: eight moons to label from a bank of new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter, each used twice. 2nd grade science PDF.
G2-367.p1: Eight moon cards fill this 2nd grade page in two columns, each with a moon on a pale square and two ruled lines beside it. A word bank at the top holds four phase names: new moon, last quarter, full moon and first quarter. The child looks at each moon and writes its name on the lines, using each name twice. On the sheet shown the moons are a full moon, a half lit on the right, a half lit on the left, a new moon, a full moon, another half lit on the left, a new moon and a half lit on the right.
G2-367.p2: The four main phases are named here, and the page makes children tell apart the two that look most alike. First quarter and last quarter are both half moons, and the only difference is which side is lit; as seen from north of the equator, first quarter is lit on the right. The name quarter confuses almost everyone, because the Moon looks half lit; it means a quarter of the way through the Moon's cycle. Crescents and gibbous moons are left out so the vocabulary stays small enough to learn well.
G2-367.p3: One sheet, eight moons, eight names. Each moon has two lines because every phase name is two words long. Use it after the moon phases in order face, which teaches the sequence without names. A calendar showing the phase symbols for the current month lets children name tonight's moon. In NGSS this sits with 1-ESS1-1, taught at grade 2 here with the words attached.

G2-368.h1: Why Do We Have Day and Night?
G2-368.title: Why Do We Have Day and Night Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-368.metaDescription: Day and night worksheet: the Sun shines on a turning Earth with six numbered pins. Decide whether each pin is in day or night and circle it in the table. 2nd grade.
G2-368.p1: A large piece of the Sun glows at the left edge of this 2nd grade page, sending three dashed arrows of light to the right. Beside it is a big circle labeled Earth, with a curved arrow at its center showing that it spins, and six numbered pins placed around the inside of the circle. Below is a table with the numbers 1 to 6 and two chips for each, Day and Night. The child looks where the Sun is and circles day or night for each pin. On the sheet shown pins 2, 4 and 5 sit on the half facing the Sun, and pins 1, 3 and 6 on the far half.
G2-368.p2: Day and night happen because the Earth turns, so each place spends part of the time facing the Sun and part facing away. This page asks children to use that idea rather than recite it. The circle is not shaded, so the child has to decide which half is lit by looking at where the light comes from; that is the reasoning the page is built on. Pins 2 and 5 sit closer to the middle than the others, so ask children to draw a line down the circle first, splitting it into the half toward the Sun and the half away.
G2-368.p3: One sheet, six pins, six circles. The Earth is labeled but drawn without land, so it reads as a plain circle; hold up a globe and point to where it would sit. A globe and a lamp in a dark room make the idea visible in minutes: stick a paper figure on the globe and turn it slowly. The full explanation of the Earth's spin belongs to NGSS 5-ESS1-2, well above this grade, so here it is the simple idea only.

G3-394.h1: Planets in Order from the Sun
G3-394.title: Planets in Order from the Sun Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free PDF
G3-394.metaDescription: Planets in order worksheet: a bank of eight planets with pictures and eight numbered lines curving out from the Sun. Write Mercury to Neptune in order. 3rd grade PDF.
G3-394.p1: A row of eight planet cards runs across the top of this 3rd grade page, each with a small drawing and a name, shuffled: Mars, Neptune, Earth, Saturn, Uranus, Jupiter, Mercury and Venus on the sheet shown. Saturn wears its rings and Uranus a thin upright ring. Below, a corner of the Sun sits at the top left, and eight numbered writing lines step down and away from it, each at the end of a dotted orbit. The child writes the name of each planet on its line, starting next to the Sun, and uses every name in the bank once.
G3-394.p2: The order of the planets is one of those facts children love to know, and this page gives it a picture: the lines step further from the Sun as the numbers go up, so distance and order are shown together. The planet drawings give clues without giving the answer away, Earth easy to recognize and the giants striped and ringed, so a child who remembers that the rocky planets come first can use the pictures to check. Pluto is not in the bank; it has been counted as a dwarf planet since 2006.
G3-394.p3: One sheet, eight planets, eight lines. A memory sentence such as My Very Eager Mother Just Served Us Noodles helps. The planets are not part of the kindergarten to grade 2 science standards, and NGSS brings the solar system in later still, so this is an enrichment page for grade 3. The giant and rocky planets face sorts the same eight planets by kind, which makes a good second page.

G3-395.title: Giant and Rocky Planets Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-395.metaDescription: Giant and rocky planets worksheet: sort ten names into giant planet, small rocky planet or not a planet. Eight planets plus the Sun and the Moon. 3rd grade PDF.
G3-395.p1: A bank of ten names sits at the top of this 3rd grade page: Neptune, Venus, Uranus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Moon, Saturn, Earth and Sun on the sheet shown. Below are three tall sorting columns, each with five writing lines: giant planet, headed by a big circle; small rocky planet, headed by a small one; and not a planet, headed by a crossed-out circle. The child sorts the names and writes each one in the right column. Four go under giant, four under rocky and two under not a planet.
G3-395.p2: Sorting the planets into two kinds is how the solar system starts to make sense: four small rocky planets close to the Sun, four giant planets of gas and ice further out. The third column is where the thinking happens. The Sun and the Moon are the two bodies children most often call planets, and giving them their own column forces a decision about what a planet is. Every column has five lines, so the number of lines does not give the answer away.
G3-395.p3: One sheet, ten names, three columns. This page is above the kindergarten to grade 2 science range and fits a grade 3 space unit; there is no NGSS standard for sorting planets at this age. Do the planets in order face first, since knowing the order makes the split plain to see: the first four are rocky, the last four giant. A scale drawing on the playground in chalk is a memorable follow-up.

G1-379.title: Map Key Worksheet for 1st Grade: Map Skills | Free Printable PDF
G1-379.metaDescription: Map key worksheet: an island park map, a key of five symbols and five boxes to count bridges, trees, benches, bushes and flower beds. 1st grade map skills PDF.
G1-379.p1: A simple island map fills the top of this 1st grade page, seen from above, with a river running down one side, a path across the middle and a north arrow in the corner. Small symbols are scattered over it. Under the map a key lists five symbols with their words: flower bed, bridge, bench, tree and bush. Below that sit five boxes headed bridge, tree, bench, bush and flower bed, one for every symbol in the key. The child finds each thing from the key on the map and writes how many there are in its box. On the sheet shown there are 1 bridge, 5 trees, 4 benches, 2 bushes and 3 flower beds.
G1-379.p2: A map key is the first real map skill: a symbol stands for a thing, and the key tells you which. Counting makes children use the key again and again, matching a small drawing to the same drawing on the map, so the idea sticks without a lecture. The tree and the bush are near look-alikes on purpose, a round leafy top and a lumpy bush, and telling them apart is where careful readers show themselves. The river and the path are drawn but not in the key, which is a good question to ask: how do you know what they are?
G1-379.p3: One sheet, five symbols, five counts. Every symbol in the key has its own box, so nothing is left over; ask children to tick each symbol on the map as they count it so none is counted twice. In the C3 Framework this supports D2.Geo.1.K-2, constructing and using maps of familiar places. Afterwards, ask children to draw a map of the classroom with a key of three symbols. The faces go on to views from above, compass roses, continents and directions on a map.

K-377.h1: Bird's-Eye View: From the Side and From Above
K-377.title: Bird's Eye View Worksheet for Kindergarten: Map Skills | Free PDF
K-377.metaDescription: Bird's eye view worksheet: five things drawn from the side, a car, mug, table, cone and chair, to match to the same things seen from above. Kindergarten map skills.
K-377.p1: Two columns face each other on this kindergarten page. The left column is headed by an eye looking sideways and shows five things drawn from the side; the right column is headed by an eye looking down and shows the same five things drawn from above, in a different order. Dots sit beside every picture, and the child draws a line from each side view to its top view. On the sheet shown the things are a car, a mug, a table, a traffic cone and a chair. From above the mug becomes a circle with a handle, the cone a dark square with rings and the chair a square with its back along one edge.
K-377.p2: Every map is a picture from above, and young children have to learn that looking down changes the shape of things. This page teaches exactly that idea and nothing else: the objects are ones a child can walk around, and the side views are the way children usually draw them. The top views keep one clue from the side, the color of the car and the cone, the handle of the mug, so children can reason from what stays the same. The table from above is just a rectangle, which is often the one children leave until last.
K-377.p3: One sheet, five things, five lines. Hold a real mug above children's heads and then at their eye level to show the change before starting. In the C3 Framework this is the beginning of D2.Geo.1.K-2, using maps of familiar places. The base map key page is the natural next step, since its symbols are small drawings seen from above, and the compass rose face follows later in grade 2.

G2-369.h1: North, East, South, West: Label the Four Directions
G2-369.title: Compass Rose Worksheet, 2nd Grade: North, East, South, West | Free PDF
G2-369.metaDescription: Compass rose worksheet: six roses, each with one letter and an orange north tip, three of them turned. Write the other three of N, E, S and W. 2nd grade map skills PDF.
G2-369.p1: Six compass roses fill this 2nd grade page in two columns, each a four-pointed star with a box at the end of every point. In each rose one box already shows a letter, N, E, S or W, the other three are empty, and one point of every star is colored orange. The child writes the missing three letters. On the sheet shown three roses stand the usual way up, with the orange point at the top, and give the child S, E or W. The other three are turned: the orange point lies to the left, to the bottom or to the right, and the given letter sits somewhere else on the rose.
G2-369.p2: Knowing north, east, south and west is not the same as knowing them in the usual picture with north at the top, and this page separates the two. The orange point always marks north, even on the turned roses, and the instruction says so, so read it aloud before children start. From north the child goes round the rose clockwise, north, east, south, west, and the given letter is the check: on the rose turned so north points left, W at the bottom confirms the order. That clockwise order is what the page really teaches, and Never Eat Soggy Waffles is the rhyme that fixes it.
G2-369.p3: One sheet, six roses, eighteen letters. Stand the class up and face each direction in the room before starting, then turn everyone a quarter turn to show that the order stays the same. Compass directions are a common grade 2 and 3 social studies unit without a Common Core standard of their own. The cardinal directions face uses the rose on a real map, which is the step after this one.

G2-370.title: Label the Continents Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-370.metaDescription: Label the continents worksheet: a world map with seven numbered continents and a bank of their names, including Oceania and Antarctica. Write each name. 2nd grade PDF.
G2-370.p1: A world map fills the top of this 2nd grade page, drawn in an oval with the land in white and the sea in pale blue. Seven orange numbers sit on the seven continents, with a dashed line marking where Europe ends and Asia begins and a pointer reaching down to Antarctica along the bottom. A bank below holds the seven names: Antarctica, Europe, Asia, North America, Oceania, Africa and South America. Seven numbered writing lanes wait at the bottom, and the child writes the name of each numbered continent on its line.
G2-370.p2: Seven continents is the count most American schools teach, and the page follows it, with National Geographic as its source. The name Oceania is used for the region that includes Australia, New Zealand and the islands around them, because the map draws all of them; many US classrooms still say Australia, so mention both names. The line between Europe and Asia is dashed because it is a border people agreed on, not a coastline, and that is a good thing to point out when children ask why Europe counts as a separate continent.
G2-370.p3: One sheet, seven continents, seven names. The numbers are shuffled, so the child cannot simply write the names from left to right. A song or a clap-along naming the seven helps before the page. Continents are a common grade 2 and 3 social studies unit without a set national standard. The continents and oceans face adds the five oceans to the same map and asks for numbers instead of names.

G3-396.title: Continents and Oceans Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-396.metaDescription: Continents and oceans worksheet: a world map with twelve numbers for seven continents and five oceans. Write each number next to its name. 3rd grade map skills PDF.
G3-396.p1: The world map of the label-the-continents page returns on this 3rd grade page, now carrying twelve numbers: seven on the continents and five in the oceans. The Pacific is numbered twice, once at each side of the map, because it wraps round behind the picture. Small pointers reach to the Arctic Ocean at the top and to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean at the bottom. Below the map sit twelve names in three columns, from Antarctica and Oceania to the Atlantic and Southern Oceans, each with a dashed box. The child finds each place on the map and writes its number next to its name.
G3-396.p2: Adding the oceans turns a list of land into a whole map, and it is where children realize that most of the world is water. The count follows National Geographic: seven continents and five oceans, with the Southern Ocean recognized in 2021, so some older materials in your room will show four oceans. Writing numbers rather than names moves the work onto the map: the names are printed, and the task is finding where each one is. The Pacific appearing twice is the moment to bring out a globe.
G3-396.p3: One sheet, twelve places, twelve numbers. This is the top of the maps family and a common grade 3 unit; continents and oceans have no Common Core standard of their own. A globe beside the page answers most questions. For a follow-up, give children a blank outline of the same map and ask for the names from memory, starting with the oceans.

G2-371.title: Cardinal Directions on a Map Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-371.metaDescription: Cardinal directions worksheet: an island map with a key, a compass rose and six rows like start at the pond, look west. Circle the one of three that lies there.
G2-371.p1: An island map fills the top of this 2nd grade page, with a compass rose beside it marked N, E, S and W and seven small symbols on the land: a tree, a pond, a bush, a flower bed, a bench, a house and a tent. A key beside the rows names all seven. Below are six numbered rows. Each starts with one of the symbols in a square, then a direction word in an orange pill, then three symbols in circles. The child finds the first picture on the map, looks the way the word says, and circles the one of the three that lies that way. All four direction words are used, two of them twice.
G2-371.p2: This face uses the compass rose for what it is for: finding things on a map. The child has to hold two things at once, where they are starting and which way the word points, and the three choices are spread across the map so only one lies in that direction. The rose sits beside the map rather than on it, so check that children read north as the top of the map before they start. There are no steps or squares to count; it is a looking task, not a route.
G2-371.p3: One sheet, six rows, six circles. The house and the tent are drawn as seen from above, a two-tone roof and a round striped tent top, and the key beside the map names them, so a quick look at the key before starting saves questions. In the C3 Framework this supports D2.Geo.1.K-2. The compass rose face is the right page to do first, and a map of the school yard with the four directions marked on it is a good follow-up.

G1-380.h1: Digraphs sh, ch and th: Which Letter Team Do You Hear?
G1-380.title: Digraphs sh, ch, th Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-380.metaDescription: Digraphs worksheet: eight pictures in a table with sh, ch and th in every row. Say the picture's name and circle the letter team you hear. Free 1st grade phonics PDF.
G1-380.p1: A table fills this 1st grade page, with three columns headed sh, ch and th and eight numbered rows, each starting with a picture. Every row repeats the three letter teams as chips, and the child says the name of the picture and circles the letter team they hear. The sheet shown runs a mushroom, a shrimp, a chair, a bar of chocolate, a jellyfish, a thumb, a bench and a feather, so sh comes up three times, ch three times and th twice. The team sits at the start of four words, in the middle of mushroom and feather, and at the end of jellyfish and bench.
G1-380.p2: A digraph is two letters that spell one sound, and sh, ch and th are the first three children meet. The page works on hearing: every row offers all three teams, so the child has to listen to the word rather than guess from a short list. Pictures carry the words, so no reading is needed, and the columns line up so a quick look down the page shows whether each sound has been found. The jellyfish is the picture to watch, since its team comes at the very end of a long word; ask children to say the whole word slowly and listen right to the last sound.
G1-380.p3: One sheet, eight pictures, eight circles. Say each word slowly with the class first and stretch the sound: shhhrimp, thhhumb. This is the base page of the digraphs family, built for the first grade phonics goal of knowing the common consonant digraphs; its faces sort pictures at kindergarten, fill in missing teams, read whole words, find where the team sits and count teams in sentences.

K-378.h1: Digraph Sort for Kindergarten: sh or ch
K-378.title: Digraph Sort Worksheet for Kindergarten: sh or ch | Free PDF
K-378.metaDescription: Digraph sort worksheet for kindergarten: six pictures down the middle, sh on one side and ch on the other. Say each name and draw a line to the team you hear.
K-378.p1: Three tall columns fill this kindergarten page. The left column is headed sh, the right column ch, and down the middle runs a line of six pictures with a dot on each side. The child says each picture's name and draws a line from the picture to the letter team they hear. The sheet shown runs a bar of chocolate, a pair of shorts, a wheelchair, a wedge of cheese, a shoe and a shrimp, three for each team, with the sound at the start of the word or of its last part.
K-378.p2: Two teams, not three, is what makes this a kindergarten page. The child only has to decide between the soft sh and the sharper ch, which is the pair young children confuse most, and every picture is a word they use every day. There is no writing and no reading; the letters are there to look at while the ears do the work. Kindergarten is readiness for digraphs rather than the year they are formally taught, so treat the page as a listening game with the letters in sight.
K-378.p3: One sheet, six pictures, six lines. Let children say sh with a finger to their lips and ch like a train before starting. The wheelchair has ch at the start of its second part, chair, so say both parts slowly. When the pair feels easy, the first grade base page adds th as a third choice, and the missing digraphs face asks children to write the teams themselves. Keep the finished sheet as a sound wall for the week.

G1-392.h1: Missing Digraphs: Write sh, ch or th
G1-392.title: Missing Digraphs Worksheet for 1st Grade: sh, ch, th | Free PDF
G1-392.metaDescription: Missing digraphs worksheet: eight picture words, like chair, wreath and beach, each missing its letter team. Write sh, ch or th in the gap. 1st grade PDF.
G1-392.p1: Three letter-team beads, sh, ch and th, sit at the top of this 1st grade page on a line like a string.
