Below are eight numbered rows, each with a picture and a word printed with a dashed gap where the team belongs. The child says the picture word and writes the missing team in the gap. On the sheet shown the words are wreath, fish, chair, thumb, thermometer, beach, wheelchair and ship, each printed with its team left out, so chair starts with the gap and wreath ends with it. The gaps sit at the start of four words, the end of three and the middle of one, in wheelchair.
G1-392.p2: Writing the team is the step from hearing a digraph to spelling it. The printed part of each word does some of the work, so the child needs only the two letters, and the picture confirms which word it is. Moving the gap around the word matters: most early practice puts digraphs at the start, and wreath, fish and beach show that the same teams also end words. Wheelchair is a compound word, so its team is really at the start of its second part, which is a helpful thing to say aloud, and chair on the same page makes the link easy to see.
G1-392.p3: One sheet, eight words, eight teams to write. The three beads stay at the top, so spelling is supported. Wreath has a silent w, so read that word with children who are still sounding out. Ask children to read each finished word back to a partner. The where is the digraph face follows naturally, since it asks the same question about position without any writing, and the read and match face turns the task around into reading whole words.

G1-393.h1: Read Digraph Words and Match the Pictures
G1-393.title: Read Digraph Words and Match Pictures, 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-393.metaDescription: Read digraph words worksheet: six words with the letter team marked, starfish, tooth, cheese, chicken, ship and feather. Draw a line to the matching picture.
G1-393.p1: Six word cards run down the left of this 1st grade page and six pictures down the right, each with a dot. In every word the letter team is marked in a pale bubble. The child reads each word and draws a line to the picture it names. On the sheet shown the words are starfish, tooth, cheese, chicken, ship and feather, and the pictures, in a different order, are a tooth, a feather, a ship, a wedge of cheese, a starfish and a chicken. The team sits at the start of three words, the end of two and the middle of one.
G1-393.p2: This is the reading face of the digraphs family. The other pages start from a picture; this one starts from print, so the child has to decode the word before the picture can help. Marking the team in each word shows the child where two letters work as one sound, which is the part of the word most likely to trip a new reader. The words are short and regular around the team, and starfish is built from two words the child may already know, so first grade readers can sound out every word from start to finish.
G1-393.p3: One sheet, six words, six lines. Read the list together first with children who are still sounding out, and let them point to the marked team as they say each word. Cheese and chicken both start with ch, so the child has to read past the team to tell them apart, which is the best moment to check real decoding. The missing digraphs face works the other way round, from picture to spelling, and the two make a good pair in one week.

G1-394.h1: Where Is the Digraph? sh, ch and th in the Word
G1-394.title: Where Is the Digraph Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-394.metaDescription: Where is the digraph worksheet: eight pictures with sh, ch or th shown. Say the word and color one of three spaces for beginning, middle or end. 1st grade phonics PDF.
G1-394.p1: Eight picture cards fill this 1st grade page in two columns. Each shows a picture, the letter team it contains in a bead above, and an arrow running left to right over three dashed ovals. The child says the picture word, listens for where the team comes, and colors one oval: the first for the beginning, the middle one for the middle and the last for the end. On the sheet shown the pictures are a sheep, a beach, a mushroom, a wheelchair, a tooth, a shovel, a sloth and an armchair.
G1-394.p2: Knowing a word has sh in it is one skill; knowing where the sound falls is another, and it is the one that helps children spell. The arrow over the ovals shows the direction of the word, so the three spaces stand for the start, the middle and the end of what the child hears. The team is given for every picture, so the page is only about position. On the sheet shown two teams come at the start, three at the end and three in the middle, in mushroom, wheelchair and armchair.
G1-394.p3: One sheet, eight pictures, eight colored spaces. Clapping or tapping along the arm as you say each word helps children find the place. Name the sheep and the sloth together before starting: the sheep is drawn young and woolly, and a child who calls it a lamb will hear no sh at all. The digraphs in sentences face is the last step, finding teams in running text.

G2-372.h1: Digraphs in Sentences: Circle and Count sh
G2-372.title: Digraphs in Sentences Worksheet for 2nd Grade: Count sh | Free PDF
G2-372.metaDescription: Digraphs in sentences worksheet: four sentences about fish, sharks and the shore. Circle every sh and write how many are in each sentence. 2nd grade phonics PDF.
G2-372.p1: One letter team, sh, sits in a large bead at the top of this 2nd grade page, and four numbered sentence cards run down below it, each with a dashed box on the right. The child reads the sentences, circles every sh, and writes how many they found in each sentence in its box. The sheet shown reads: A fish swims to the dish. The shark and the fish splash in the sea. My cat sat in the shade. A crab ran up the shore to the shed. There are eight to find, in fish, dish, shark, fish, splash, shade, shore and shed.
G2-372.p2: Finding a team inside running text is harder than finding it in one picture word, and it is a step toward reading fluently: the child has to notice sh in the middle of a sentence without being told which word holds it. The sentences are simple and decodable, so the counting is the challenge. Swims and sea start with s but not with sh, and a careful reader will not circle them; that is the distinction the page is really testing.
G2-372.p3: One sheet, four sentences, four counts. The first grade digraphs are reviewed here at grade 2, so treat it as a quick fluency check rather than new learning. Children who finish can write their own sh sentence and swap it with a partner to count. Reading the sentences aloud after circling lets children hear every team they found. This is the last face of the digraphs family and the only one built on running text.

G2-358.h1: Synonyms: Circle the Word That Means the Same
G2-358.title: Synonyms Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-358.metaDescription: Synonyms worksheet: eight cards, each a big word like quiet or grumpy above four choices. Circle the one that means the same, from hushed to calm. 2nd grade PDF.
G2-358.p1: Eight numbered cards fill this 2nd grade page in two columns. Each card has one big word in a pale band at the top and four words in chips below it, and the child circles the one that means the same as the big word. On the sheet shown the big words are quiet, shut, yell, jump, amazed, noisy, peaceful and grumpy, and the words to find are hushed, close, shout, leap, astonished, loud, calm and angry. The other three chips on each card are words with a different meaning altogether, such as sleepy, lovely and yummy under quiet.
G2-358.p2: A synonym is a word that means the same, or nearly the same, as another, and second graders are asked to notice how words relate. The page keeps the task clean: on every card only one choice is close in meaning, and the others are unrelated rather than opposites, so the page does not blur synonyms with antonyms. Some pairs are exact, like shut and close; others are near, like grumpy and angry, where angry is stronger. That difference is worth a word, and the shades of meaning face is built on it.
G2-358.p3: One sheet, eight cards, eight circles. Say each pair in a sentence to check it, shut the door and close the door. This is the base page of the synonyms family, and it owns the plain task of finding the word that means the same; the faces add pictures, matching pairs, shades of meaning, words for said and word fields. A class chart of the eight pairs keeps the new words in sight for the week.

G1-395.h1: Synonyms with Pictures: Two Words, One Picture
G1-395.title: Synonyms with Pictures Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-395.metaDescription: Synonyms with pictures worksheet: six pictures, each above four words. Circle the two that mean the same and tell about it, like big and large for a whale.
G1-395.p1: Six picture cards fill this 1st grade page. Each shows one picture in a frame at the top, with a small linked-rings mark in the corner, and four words underneath. The child circles the two words that mean the same and tell about the picture. The sheet shown has a scared face, a whale, a racing car, a sleepy face with zzz beside it, an angry face and a happy face, and the pairs to find are afraid and scared, big and large, quick and speedy, tired and sleepy, angry and grumpy, and glad and cheerful.
G1-395.p2: The picture does the defining here. A first grader who does not yet know the word speedy can look at the racing car, find quick, and see that speedy sits beside it meaning the same thing, so the page teaches a new word through a known one. The two wrong words on each card are real describing words from other cards, so the child has to check each word against the picture rather than pick the longest. Four of the six pictures are faces showing a feeling, because feelings are where young children most need more than one word.
G1-395.p3: One sheet, six pictures, twelve circles. The whale is drawn as a friendly cartoon, so talk about how big a real whale is when you reach big and large. This face is readiness for the grade 2 synonym work and uses easier words than the base page. A good follow-up is to hold up a picture from a class book and ask for two words that tell about it.

G2-373.h1: Synonym Pairs: Match the Words That Mean the Same
G2-373.title: Synonym Pairs Matching Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-373.metaDescription: Synonym pairs worksheet: eight words on the left and eight on the right. Draw a line linking each pair that means the same, like weep and cry. 2nd grade PDF.
G2-373.p1: Two columns of eight word cards face each other on this 2nd grade page, each card with a small clasp shape on its inner edge and a dot beside it. The child draws a line to link each word on the left with the word on the right that means the same. The left column on the sheet shown reads yummy, tumble, speak, scared, happy, weep, hushed and cluttered, and the right column, in a different order, reads cry, messy, fall, cheerful, quiet, delicious, frightened and talk.
G2-373.p2: Matching replaces the choice among four with a closed set: every word on the right is somebody's partner, so the child can work by elimination once a few pairs are secure. That builds confidence, and the page adds difficulty in the words themselves: hushed, cluttered and tumble are words second graders may not know yet, and matching them to quiet, messy and fall is how they learn them. The pairs are all close synonyms rather than near ones, and none of the right-hand words is a trap.
G2-373.p3: One sheet, sixteen words, eight lines. Encourage children to start with the pairs they are sure of and leave the hard ones for last, and to draw with a ruler so the page stays readable when lines cross. Several words also appear on the base page, quiet and hushed among them, so doing both in one week reinforces them. The synonyms for said face is a good next step, where the word has to fit a sentence.

G1-396.h1: Shades of Meaning: From a Little to a Lot
G1-396.title: Shades of Meaning Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-396.metaDescription: Shades of meaning worksheet: six rows of three words, like warm, hot and boiling. Write 1, 2 and 3 from the weakest word to the strongest. 1st grade vocabulary PDF.
G1-396.p1: Six rows of three words fill this 1st grade page, each word with a dashed box beneath it. A key at the top shows three bars growing from pale and short to dark and tall, numbered 1, 2 and 3, and a small copy of the bars starts every row. The child reads the three words and writes 1, 2 and 3 to order them from the weakest to the strongest. The six word sets are tap, knock and bang; damp, wet and soaked; sip, drink and gulp; nibble, eat and gobble; like, love and adore; and warm, hot and boiling, each printed in mixed order.
G1-396.p2: Shades of meaning is the first grade idea that words for the same thing can be stronger or weaker. The page uses action words and describing words together: tap, knock and bang are all ways of hitting a door, but they are not equal. The words in each row are mixed up, so the child cannot simply copy 1, 2 and 3 from left to right. Acting out a row is the quickest way to settle an argument: sip, drink and gulp a cup of water and the order is obvious.
G1-396.p3: One sheet, six rows, eighteen numbers. Some rows invite debate, and knock versus tap is a good one to leave open if a child can defend their order. This face is the first grade entry to the synonyms family; the grade 2 base page asks for words that mean the same, and this one shows that the same is often only nearly the same. A thermometer drawn on the board makes a good anchor for warm, hot and boiling.

G2-374.h1: Synonyms for Said: Pick the Word That Fits
G2-374.title: Synonyms for Said Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-374.metaDescription: Synonyms for said worksheet: six sentences with a gap and a bubble of six words: answered, explained, whispered, shouted, asked, promised. Write the best fit.
G2-374.p1: A speech bubble at the top of this 2nd grade page holds said, crossed out, and six other words: answered, explained, whispered, shouted, asked and promised. Six numbered sentences below each have a dashed box where a speaking word belongs, and the child writes the one from the bubble that fits best. On the sheet shown the sentences include The bus was leaving, so Lily ..., “Wait for me!” and "I have a secret for you," Max ... into Grandma's ear, and each word in the bubble is used once.
G2-374.p2: Said is the word every young writer overuses, and replacing it is one of the first vocabulary lessons in writing. Every sentence on the page would still make sense with said in the gap, which is exactly the point: the child swaps a plain word for a more exact one. The sentences carry the clue: a bus leaving means shouting, a secret into Grandma's ear means whispering, a question mark means asking, a promise about every day means promising. The last two rows are the ones to discuss: Emma gives the steps one by one, so she explains, and Leo speaks right after the teacher's question, so he answers.
G2-374.p3: One sheet, six sentences, six words. Ask children to read the finished sentences aloud in the voice the word suggests, which makes the difference between whispered and shouted impossible to miss. Keep a class list of said words on the wall and add to it through the year. The word fields face at grade 3 does the same thing for go and look.

G3-397.h1: Word Fields: Words for Go and Look
G3-397.title: Word Fields Worksheet for 3rd Grade: Go and Look | Free Printable PDF
G3-397.metaDescription: Word fields worksheet: ten verbs, from stroll and hurry to peek and observe, to sort into the go field and the look field. Write each on a line. 3rd grade PDF.
G3-397.p1: A bank of ten verbs sits at the top of this 3rd grade page: squint, creep, stroll, gaze, hurry, peek, glance, observe, walk and watch on the sheet shown. Below are two tall panels, each topped with a small fence and headed by a word in quotation marks, go on the left and look on the right, with six writing lines in each. The child writes each word in the field it belongs to. Four words belong to go and six to look, and both fields have the same number of lines, so the lines do not give the answer away.
G3-397.p2: A word field groups words that share a core meaning, and it is a way of seeing vocabulary as families of ideas rather than a list. Go and look are the two most useful fields at this age, because children use the plain words constantly and have many better ones available: creep, stroll and hurry are all going, but at very different speeds; peek, glance and gaze are all looking, for very different lengths of time. Observe is the word to talk about, since it is the one science will ask them to use.
G3-397.p3: One sheet, ten words, two fields. For a stretch, ask children to rank the look words from quickest to longest, which joins this page to the shades of meaning face. The synonyms for said face is the grade 2 version of the same idea with speaking words. This is the top of the synonyms family, and a good lead into story writing, where every walk can become something more exact.

G2-359.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G2-359.h1: Root Words: Sort by the Root
G2-359.title: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet, 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-359.metaDescription: Root words worksheet: ten words built on play and help, from replay to helplessly. Write each on the wall that stands on its root. 2nd grade prefixes and suffixes PDF.
G2-359.p1: Ten word tiles sit at the top of this 2nd grade page: helplessly, replay, playfully, helper, playtime, helpfully, helpful, player, helpless and playful on the sheet shown. Below stand two walls of five dashed lines each, built on a foundation stone: play on the left, help on the right. The child reads each word and writes it on a line of the wall that stands on its root word. Five go on each wall. The words carry the prefix re- and the suffixes -ful, -less, -er and -ly, and several carry two endings at once.
G2-359.p2: A root word is the part that carries the meaning, and prefixes and suffixes are added to it to change that meaning. Seeing that helper, helpful, helpless and helplessly all stand on help is the second grade skill of using a known root to work out a new word. The walls make it visual: every word is literally built on its root. Replay is the tile to point at, because it is the only one where the root does not come first, and a child who sorts by the first letters alone will put it in the wrong place.
G2-359.p3: One sheet, ten words, two walls. Playtime is a compound word, two whole words joined, rather than a root with an ending, which is worth a sentence since compound words have a family of their own. This is the base page of the prefixes, suffixes and root words family; its faces use pictures, find the shared root, choose prefixes by meaning, build person words and fit a family into sentences.

G1-397.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G1-397.h1: Root Words with Pictures: Circle the Word
G1-397.title: Root Words with Pictures Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-397.metaDescription: Root words with pictures worksheet: six pictures, tooth, fish, cloud, book, flower and hand, each under three words. Circle the one built from the picture word.
G1-397.p1: Six cards fill this 1st grade page in two rows. Each shows a picture in a frame at the bottom and three words in boxes above it, and the child names the picture, then circles the one word above it that is built from that picture word. On the sheet shown the pictures are a tooth, a fish, a cloud, a book, a flower and a hand, and the words to find are toothy, fishy, cloudy, booklet, flowery and handy. The other words on each card start with the same letters but are not built from the picture: tomato and toad, fist and first, clown and close.
G1-397.p2: This is readiness for the root words family, the first time a child sees that one word can grow out of another. The picture gives the root without any reading, and the three choices look alike on purpose, so the child has to check that the whole picture word is inside the longer word, not just its first letters. Most of the answers add -y, and booklet adds -let, so the page also shows that different endings can grow from a word. Hammer and hamster are close traps on the last card, since both start like hand but neither holds it.
G1-397.p3: One sheet, six pictures, six circles. The flower card is the tricky one, because flour sounds exactly like flower but is not built from it; a child who circles it is listening well and reading less, so ask them to look at the spelling. The find the root word face is the grade 2 version, where the child sees three family members and has to find the root without a picture.

G2-375.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G2-375.title: Find the Root Word Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-375.metaDescription: Find the root word worksheet: nine cards of three related words, like careful, careless and carelessly. Circle the shared part and write the root in the stone.
G2-375.p1: Nine cards fill this 2nd grade page in three rows. Each holds three related words and an empty stone at the bottom. The first card is worked as an example: cheerful, cheerfully and cheerily have cheer circled in each, and cheer is written in the stone. On every other card the child circles the part the three words share and writes that root word in the stone. On the sheet shown the roots to find are use, play, act, power, joy, care, sleep and rest, in words that run from misuse and replay to enjoyment, restlessness and sleepover.
G2-375.p2: Finding the root is the reverse of the base page. There the root was given and the child sorted words onto it; here the family is given and the child has to find what holds it together. The words are chosen so that the root is not always at the start: misuse, replay, enjoy and asleep put something in front of it. Card six is a good one to discuss, since enjoy is itself a word, but the part all three of its words share is joy.
G2-375.p3: One sheet, nine cards, eight roots to find. Some of the words are compound words rather than a root with endings, sleepover and armrest among them, which is worth mentioning if your class has already met compound words. Ask children to add a fourth word to any card they finish early. The prefixes by meaning face comes next and looks closely at the front of the word.

G2-376.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G2-376.h1: Prefixes re-, pre- and mis-: Pick by Meaning
G2-376.title: Prefixes re, pre, mis Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-376.metaDescription: Prefixes worksheet: a key of re-, pre- and mis- with their meanings and eight definitions like to fill an empty cup back up. Write the prefix in front of each base word.
G2-376.p1: A key at the top of this 2nd grade page shows three puzzle pieces, re, pre and mis, with their meanings underneath: again, before and wrongly. Eight numbered rows follow, each with a short definition on the left and a two-piece word on the right: an empty dashed piece in front of a base word such as fill, view, place, pay, read, count, heat and spell. The child reads what the new word means, finds its prefix in the key and writes it in the empty piece. On the sheet shown each prefix is needed two or three times, making refill, preview, misplace, prepay, reread, miscount, preheat and misspell.
G2-376.p2: Knowing what a prefix means lets a child work out a word they have never seen, and re-, pre- and mis- are three of the most common. The puzzle pieces make the idea physical: the prefix clicks onto the front of a word and changes its meaning. The definitions are written in everyday words rather than the key's own, back up and one more time for again, early and first for before, so the child has to translate the meaning before choosing. The mis- rows say not right instead of wrongly, so no row can be solved by spotting the same letters in the definition and the key.
G2-376.p3: One sheet, eight definitions, eight prefixes. Misspell is a good one to spell out together, since the double s surprises children. Afterwards, write the three prefixes on the board and ask the class for new words for each. This face works on the front of the word; the person word face looks at an ending, and the base page mixes both.

G3-398.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G3-398.h1: Who Does It? The Person Word
G3-398.title: Person Words Worksheet for 3rd Grade: Who Does It? | Free Printable PDF
G3-398.metaDescription: Person words worksheet: eight people beside a word like teach, bake or farm. Write the person word in the empty brick: teacher, baker, farmer. 3rd grade suffix PDF.
G3-398.p1: Eight cards fill this 3rd grade page in two columns. Each shows a person doing something on the left and, on the right, a word in a box above an empty brick with a writing line. The child looks at the person, reads the word beside them and writes the person word in the brick. On the sheet shown the words are run, photograph, dance, garden, teach, bake, farm and sing, and the pictures show a girl running, a boy with a camera, a ballet dancer, a gardener with a spade, a teacher with a clipboard, a baker with a loaf, a young farmer with a pitchfork and a boy singing with a guitar.
G3-398.p2: Adding an ending to make a person word is one of the most useful suffix patterns: teach becomes teacher, bake becomes baker, farm becomes farmer. All eight words on this sheet take -er, and the interest is in the small spelling changes that come with it: the dropped e of baker and dancer, the doubled n of runner, and photographer, where the ending joins a long word without any change at all. Say each finished word aloud and listen for how the ending keeps the same sound every time.
G3-398.p3: One sheet, eight words, eight person words to write. Several pictures show children rather than grown-ups at work, the runner, the photographer and the singer among them, so talk about a person word as someone who does something, whether or not it is their job. This face is above the second grade band of the family and fits grade 3 suffix work. The root words in sentences face is its natural companion.

G3-399.eyebrow: Prefixes, Suffixes and Root Words Worksheet
G3-399.title: Root Words in Sentences Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-399.metaDescription: Root words in sentences worksheet: two word families, joy and sleep, four words each. Write enjoy, joyful, sleepy or sleeper into the sentence it fits. 3rd grade.
G3-399.p1: Two panels fill this 3rd grade page, each built around one root word on a stone: joy in the first and sleep in the second. Above each stone sit four words from its family, enjoy, enjoyment, joyful and joyfully in the first panel and sleepiness, sleepily, sleepy and sleeper in the second. Below each stone are four sentences with a gap, and the child writes each of the four words into the sentence it fits. On the sheet shown the sentences include The dog jumped ... when we came home, We read the funny story for pure ..., and Our baby is a light ... and wakes at every sound.
G3-399.p2: Knowing a word family is one step; using the right member in a sentence is the harder one, and it depends on grammar as much as meaning. Joyful describes, joyfully tells how, enjoyment names a thing and enjoy is an action, and each sentence only accepts one of them. That makes this page a quiet grammar lesson inside a vocabulary page: the ending tells the child what job the word will do. A light sleeper is the sentence most likely to need talking about.
G3-399.p3: One sheet, two families, eight sentences. Each panel uses all four of its words once, so the last gap in each panel can be checked by elimination. Sleepiness carries two endings at once, -y and then -ness, which is worth pointing out as the longest word on the page. This is the top of the prefixes, suffixes and root words family and a natural place to ask children to write a sentence of their own for one more word from either family.
